method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: Two Federal Reserve officials, St. Louis's Alberto Musalem and Dallas's Lorie Logan, said on Friday that rates still need to rise, after strong growth and inflation figures this week. But a steep fall in tech shares over AI spending pushed money into US bonds and pulled yields down, so the dollar ended the week slightly softer, near 101.6 on its index.

EUR.text: The European Central Bank hinted at a December rate rise on Thursday, and the euro zone grew 0.4% last quarter, twice the forecast, while prices jumped in Italy and France. But German inflation cooled to 2.8%, France's economy shrank and Fitch warned late Friday it may cut France's credit rating, so the euro sits near $1.117 and keeps losing ground to the pound.

GBP.text: The pound led the major currencies on Friday, above $1.34 and at its strongest against the euro this year, after a Bank of England survey showed firms expecting faster price rises. Chancellor John Healey's first budget passed without a bond-market scare, and the Bank of England decision on November 5, where a rise is widely expected, is what could move it next.

JPY.text: The Bank of Japan held its rate at 1.25% on Friday but said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal, and one board member wanted a rise straight away, so a December hike looks likely. Friday's tech-led stock sell-off and lower US yields add shelter demand near 157 per dollar, though oil near $118 a barrel keeps weighing on Japan.

CHF.text: The Swiss franc draws shelter money when stocks fall, as in Friday's worst US stock day since June, and when Iran attacks ships near Hormuz. President Trump's talk of the war ending soon pulls the other way, and Swiss rates far below US rates keep pressure running both ways.

CAD.text: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on Wednesday, its first hike in three years, and oil above $100 a barrel, a big Canadian export, has the loonie just under 1.40 per US dollar. But Friday's figures showed the economy flat in August and likely shrinking in September, well below the bank's forecast, which makes another rise harder to justify.

AUD.text: Hot Australian inflation means markets see a strong chance the Reserve Bank of Australia raises rates again on November 3, which supports the Australian dollar near 70 US cents. But China, Australia's biggest customer, saw factory and service activity shrink in October, and Friday's slide in world stocks also weighs.

NZD.text: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by keeping its rate at 2.75% on October 28 instead of raising it, so the kiwi has lost its rate support and sits near 56 US cents. Weaker-than-expected Chinese business surveys, a key market for New Zealand's dairy, add to the drag.

XAU.text: Gold fell more than 3% on Friday to below $3,900 an ounce, its lowest in a year and some 30% under January's record, as Fed officials talked up more rate rises and some investors sold it to cover stock losses. Central-bank buying and the Iran war have not been enough to stop a second monthly fall.

OIL.text: Brent crude closed Friday near $118 a barrel, its highest since April, and rose about 14% in October. Iran says four tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday alone, and traders fear new fighting after the US midterms on November 3, even though President Trump says the war will end soon.

items.headline: Chinese NBS Manufacturing PMI (Oct) 49.3 vs. Exp. 50 (Prev. 50.1)
items.story_title: China: a slowing economy
items.summary: China's official business surveys for October fell below the 50 line that splits growth from shrinking, for both factories and services, and both missed forecasts.

beats.was: China's National Bureau of Statistics publishes monthly purchasing managers' surveys, where readings above 50 mean activity is growing. In September both factories (50.1) and services and construction (50.2) were just above that line.
beats.happened: On Saturday the factory reading dropped to 49.3, against 50.0 expected, and the services and construction reading fell to 49.7, against 50.5 expected. The combined measure slid to 49.7 from 50.7, with weak demand, including for exports, blamed.
beats.means: The world's second-largest economy slipped back into shrinking across the board in October, with costly oil and softer overseas orders weighing. It raises the odds Beijing adds more support.
beats.fx: China buys much of Australia's iron ore and much of New Zealand's dairy, so a weaker China tends to weigh on both their currencies, and on demand for oil and metals.

impact.why: China is Australia's biggest customer, and both factory and service activity there shrank more than expected.
Softer Chinese demand is a worry for New Zealand's exports.
Shrinking Chinese activity trims hopes for oil demand, though war supply worries dominate for now.

items.watch: China's private-sector surveys early next week and any sign Beijing steps up spending or rate cuts.

items.headline: Oil jumps 2pc
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Oil closed Friday at its highest since late April and gained about 14% in October, as traders braced for the Iran war to flare again after next week's US elections.

beats.was: Oil has climbed for four months as the war with Iran disrupts Gulf shipping, even though Gulf exports have recovered by sending more crude around the Strait of Hormuz.
beats.happened: Brent crude for December, which expired on Friday, settled up 2.4% at $117.64 a barrel after touching $118; US crude settled near $104. Brent rose 13.6% over October and US crude 15.2%. Maritime sources called a tanker hit by a small boat's explosives the first successful limpet-mine attack in the strait since the war began.
beats.means: Oil is ending the month near its highs, with traders paying up in case fighting resumes after the November 3 midterms. Qatari mediators are back in Tehran, but Iran has yet to answer a US letter.
beats.fx: Dear oil supports Canada's dollar and keeps pressure on oil importers such as Japan and the euro zone, while feeding inflation worries that keep rate-rise talk alive.

impact.why: Prices closed at a six-month high on fears of new fighting after the midterms.
Higher crude prices help Canada's export earnings.
A bigger oil import bill weighs on Japan.

items.watch: Any reply from Iran to the US letter, and tanker traffic through the strait when markets reopen.

items.headline: IRGC says fourth tanker hit mine in Strait of Hormuz
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a fourth tanker in a single day caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a supertanker carrying over 2 million barrels, and Britain's maritime agency reported a separate ship hit by a projectile.

beats.was: Since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, Iran has limited traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea route for much of the world's oil, and says ships must use routes it approves.
beats.happened: Late on Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards navy said a supertanker leaving by a southern route it calls unauthorised struck a mine and caught fire, the fourth tanker fire since Friday began. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said an unknown projectile hit a ship about 40 nautical miles south of Iran's Lavan Island; the crew was safe.
beats.means: Iran is showing it can still threaten ships that defy it, even as the US says it has cleared Iranian mines from the strait. Each new attack lifts insurance and freight costs for Gulf oil.
beats.fx: More danger to Gulf shipping supports oil prices, which helps oil exporters like Canada and hurts big importers like Japan, and it can draw money into havens such as the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Repeated tanker strikes in the main Gulf export route keep supply fears high.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude hurts its trade balance.
Rising war risk tends to draw shelter money to the franc.
Higher oil prices help Canada, a big crude exporter.

items.watch: Whether shipping firms confirm the strikes, and whether tanker traffic through the strait slows over the weekend.

items.headline: Fitch revises France's outlook to 'negative' on worsening debt dynamics
items.story_title: France: rising debt and a budget fight
items.summary: Credit rating agency Fitch warned it may cut France's rating, changing its outlook to negative because debt keeps climbing and politics make cuts hard.

beats.was: France is struggling to pass next year's budget amid street protests, its economy shrank last quarter, and its 10-year borrowing cost rose above 5.1% last week, the highest since 2002.
beats.happened: Late on Friday Fitch moved France's outlook from stable to negative, pointing to weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit since August. It expects debt to reach about 124% of the economy by 2028, up from about 116% last year.
beats.means: A negative outlook is a warning that a downgrade could follow. It adds pressure on French bonds just as Paris needs to show it can cut its deficit before the next presidential election.
beats.fx: Worry about France's debt can push its borrowing costs up relative to Germany's, which tends to weigh on the euro, though the effect is usually small unless a downgrade actually comes.

impact.why: A step toward a French downgrade adds to doubts about the euro zone's second-largest economy.

items.watch: How French bonds trade on Monday after weekend protests, and whether the budget makes it through parliament.

items.headline: THE CLOSING BELL: Wall Street drops to its worst day since June after the sell-off for tech stocks deepens
items.story_title: Wall Street: doubts over AI spending
items.summary: US stocks had their worst day since June on Friday as doubts about the payoff from heavy AI spending spread, while investors bought government bonds and pushed yields lower.

beats.was: Big US tech firms have been spending huge sums on AI data centres, and this week's earnings from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel raised doubts about when that spending pays off.
beats.happened: The S&P 500 fell 1.8%, a third weekly loss, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 2.9%. Intel dropped about 29%, its worst day since 1974, after a weak forecast. The 10-year US Treasury yield slipped to 4.93%, down from above 5.30% earlier in October.
beats.means: Fear is spreading from a few AI names to the wider market just before Tuesday's US midterm elections. Falling bond yields show money hiding in safer assets.
beats.fx: Lower US yields take away some of the dollar's rate support, while stock-market stress usually helps the yen and the Swiss franc and hurts riskier currencies like the Australian dollar.

impact.why: Stock-market stress and lower US yields tend to help the yen.
Lower yields weigh on the dollar, but shelter demand for US bonds pulls the other way.
A broad stock sell-off tends to draw money to the franc.
The Australian dollar usually falls when global stocks slide.

items.watch: Whether the sell-off spreads in Asia on Monday and how markets treat Tuesday's midterm results.

items.headline: Fed needs at least two more rate hikes, Logan says
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who votes on rates this year, said the Fed should raise rates at least twice more, by a quarter point each, and then pause to take stock.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve kept its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday in a 10-2 vote, and Chair Kevin Warsh declined to promise a rise in December even after strong growth and inflation figures.
beats.happened: Logan, who backed Wednesday's hold, told students at Davidson College that rates should end at least half a point higher to bring inflation back to 2%, and that skipping one meeting does not change where policy is heading. Earlier in the day St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said a rise is needed soon.
beats.means: Two policymakers in one day are now pushing for more rises, and Logan put a number on it, which makes a December rise and at least one more after it easier to price.
beats.fx: A higher path for US rates supports the dollar and weighs on gold, though falling bond yields on stock-market worries blunted the effect on Friday.

impact.why: A voting Fed official calling for two more rises firms up the case for higher US rates.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: If Warsh or other voters push back on a set path, or US jobs figures next week come in weak, the case for two more rises fades.

items.headline: Gold Crashes Below $3,900 to One-Year Low Even as Global Stock Markets Plunge
items.story_title: Gold: sliding as Fed rate-rise bets build
items.summary: Gold fell about 3% on Friday to just under $3,900 an ounce, its lowest in a year, even as stocks sold off, which would normally help it.

beats.was: Gold peaked near $5,600 in January and had been drifting lower as hot US inflation figures raised the odds of another Federal Reserve rate rise in December.
beats.happened: Spot gold dropped about 3.1% to roughly $3,897, leaving it some 30% below its record; silver fell about 6% to under $50 for the first time in nearly a year. Analysts quoted by Reuters suggested some investors sold gold to cover losses on falling tech shares.
beats.means: Rising US rate expectations and oil-driven inflation worries are outweighing gold's usual pull as a safe place in a sell-off, and forced selling made the drop sharper.
beats.fx: Clear pressure on gold; the selling is about higher US rates rather than a stronger dollar, which was softer on the day.

impact.why: A one-year low on bets for higher US rates and selling to cover stock losses.

items.watch: If US stocks steady and the margin-call selling stops, or Fed officials soften their talk of more rises, gold could find a floor.

items.headline: Fed's Musalem says a rate hike is needed 'soon'
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said the Fed will need to raise rates again, and soon, because inflation is still too high.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday after a rise in September, and Chair Kevin Warsh would not say what comes in December.
beats.happened: Musalem, who does not vote on rates this year but will next year, said in a speech that policy is still too loose to bring inflation down to 2% and that small, early rises are safer than bigger ones later.
beats.means: He adds his voice to the officials pushing for a December rise, and argues it can be done without hurting jobs or growth.
beats.fx: Talk of more Fed rises supports the dollar, though on Friday a stock sell-off pulling bond yields lower largely offset it.

impact.why: Another Fed official backing a near-term rise supports US rates, but he has no vote this year.
Higher expected US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less appealing.

items.watch: The US jobs report on November 6; a weak one would make a December rise harder to argue for.

items.headline: Iran war will 'get wrapped up soon', Trump says
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: President Donald Trump said the war with Iran will end soon and that the US won't strike Iran before Tuesday's midterm elections, but gave no timeline or plan.

beats.was: Reports this week said the head of US Central Command briefed Trump on options for new strikes on Iran, possibly after the November 3 midterm elections, while Qatar tries to restart talks.
beats.happened: In a Kansas City radio interview on Friday, Trump said the war will be 'wrapped up soon' and that the US needs a guarantee Iran will never get a nuclear weapon. He said there would be no strikes before the midterms and that petrol prices would fall once the war ends.
beats.means: The comments rule out action in the next few days but leave the period after the elections open. Markets did not take them as a sign of an imminent deal; oil rose on the day.
beats.fx: Talk of an end to the war tends to ease oil and lift riskier currencies, but with no details it does little against the tanker attacks.

impact.why: Talk of the war ending soon offers some relief, though without a plan.
Less near-term war risk trims shelter demand slightly.

items.watch: Whether talks with Iran restart through Qatar, and what Washington signals after Tuesday's vote.

items.headline: Canada's Economy Flatlined Again In August
items.story_title: Canada: a stalling economy after the rate rise
items.summary: Canada's economy did not grow in August for a second month running, short of the small gain forecast, and an early read points to a dip in September.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on October 28, its first rise in three years, betting the economy could take it; it expected growth near 2% a year.
beats.happened: Statistics Canada said output was flat in August against a forecast 0.2% gain, with wholesale trade down 1.4%, and its early estimate shows a 0.1% fall in September. That leaves the third quarter growing at only about 1.3% a year.
beats.means: Growth is running well below what the central bank assumed when it raised rates, which makes another rise harder to justify soon.
beats.fx: Less room for more hikes → mild weight on the Canadian dollar, though oil above $100 is holding it up for now.

impact.why: Weaker growth than the Bank of Canada expected cools talk of another rate rise.

items.watch: If Bank of Canada officials brush off the weak figures and repeat that more rises may be needed, the loonie's support returns.

items.headline: Euro Zone Economic Growth Surpasses Forecasts Despite Energy Headwinds
items.story_title: Euro zone: growth holds up as prices climb
items.summary: The euro zone economy grew 0.4% in the third quarter, twice what economists expected, even as France shrank and Italy stalled.

beats.was: High energy costs from the Iran war have squeezed Europe, and the European Central Bank held its rate at 2.5% on Thursday while hinting at a December rise.
beats.happened: Output rose 0.4% on the quarter and 1.3% on the year, both above forecast, though slower than the 0.6% of the quarter before. Germany grew 0.2%, Spain 0.6% and Ireland 5.5%, while Italy was flat and France slipped 0.1%.
beats.means: A sturdier economy gives the central bank more room to raise rates to fight inflation. Ireland's jump flatters the total, and France's slide shows the strain underneath.
beats.fx: Better growth backs a December rate rise → support for the euro.

impact.why: Growth twice the forecast makes a December rate rise easier for the central bank.

items.watch: Weak business surveys next week, or energy prices jumping again, would undo the growth story.

items.headline: Italy October preliminary CPI +5.4% vs +4.6% y/y expected
items.story_title: Euro zone: growth holds up as prices climb
items.summary: Italian inflation jumped to 5.4% in October from 4.2%, far above the 4.6% expected, as energy bills surged.

beats.was: Energy prices across Europe have climbed since the Iran war closed much of the Strait of Hormuz, and the European Central Bank is weighing a December rate rise.
beats.happened: Italy's statistics office said consumer prices rose 5.4% over the year in October, and 5.6% on the European measure. Regulated energy prices were up nearly 60%, and goods prices rose 7.5%.
beats.means: Earlier on Friday France also came in hotter than expected, so October inflation for the whole euro zone looks likely to rise again, adding pressure on the central bank to raise rates.
beats.fx: Hotter inflation → stronger case for a December rise → support for the euro.

impact.why: A big inflation surprise in the zone's third-largest economy raises the odds of a December rate rise.

items.watch: If the euro-zone-wide inflation figure comes in softer than these country prints suggest, the push for a December rise would ease.

items.headline: DXY softer with G10s broadly firmer; GBP leads as EUR/GBP prints a fresh 2026 low, USD/JPY dips after the BoJ
items.story_title: Bank of England: a rate rise in November?
items.summary: The pound led the major currencies on Friday, rising above $1.34 and to its strongest level against the euro this year, as a softer dollar lifted most others.

beats.was: The Bank of England meets on November 5, and a rate rise is widely expected because UK inflation has been pushed up by energy costs from the Iran war.
beats.happened: Sterling climbed above $1.34 and the euro fell to about 0.834 pounds, a 2026 low. A Bank of England survey of firms showed they expect prices to rise 3.3% over the next year, up from 3.1%, and UK house prices held flat in October.
beats.means: Firms expecting faster price rises makes a November rate rise easier to justify, and the pound is gaining against a euro weighed by France's shrinking economy.
beats.fx: Rising price expectations and a likely rate rise → support for the pound, most clearly against the euro.

impact.why: Top performer among majors and a fresh 2026 high against the euro ahead of a likely rate rise.
Lost ground to the pound despite firm euro-zone figures.
The dollar index edged lower again, near 101.6 to 101.9.

items.watch: A softer UK inflation reading or Bank of England officials playing down a November rise would cool the pound's run.

items.headline: German Inflation Looked Softer In October, State By State
items.story_title: Euro zone: growth holds up as prices climb
items.summary: Inflation cooled in Germany's biggest states in October, pointing to a dip in the national rate even as Italy and France ran hotter.

beats.was: German inflation rose to 3.3% in September, its highest since late 2023, on energy costs from the Iran war, and the European Central Bank has hinted at a December rate rise.
beats.happened: Early state figures showed prices up 2.8% over the year in Bavaria (from 3.2%) and 2.7% in North Rhine-Westphalia (from 3.3%), with Lower Saxony and Baden-Wuerttemberg also lower. Economists expect the national rate to ease to about 3.1%.
beats.means: Germany, the euro zone's largest economy, may be cooling while Italy and France heat up, which softens the case for a December rise a little.
beats.fx: Cooler German prices → slightly less pressure on the central bank to raise rates → a small drag on the euro.

impact.why: Softer prices in the biggest economy take a little heat out of the December rate-rise case.

items.watch: A national German figure well below 3.1%, or a soft euro-zone figure next Wednesday, would weaken the case for a December rise.

items.headline: Swiss KOF Barometer Falls in October
items.story_title: Switzerland: economy and the franc
items.summary: A closely watched gauge of Switzerland's economic outlook slipped in October and missed forecasts, though it stays above its long-run average.

beats.was: The Swiss franc has drawn shelter money during the Iran war, and Swiss interest rates are far below those in the US.
beats.happened: The KOF economic barometer, a monthly forecast gauge from Zurich's ETH university, fell to 107.6 from 109.1, below the 108.3 expected. The drop was broad, though factories added to it.
beats.means: Switzerland's outlook is still solid, just a little less upbeat, which gives the Swiss National Bank no new reason to change course.
beats.fx: Slight miss but still strong → little lasting pressure on the franc.

impact.why: A small miss on the outlook gauge, from a still-healthy level.

items.watch: A sharper fall in next month's gauge or weak Swiss inflation figures would raise talk of easier Swiss policy.

items.headline: Analysts react to BOJ decision to keep rates steady
items.story_title: Bank of Japan: how soon the next rate rise
items.summary: The Bank of Japan kept its rate at 1.25% on Friday, but said for the first time that underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal, which keeps a December rise firmly on the table.

beats.was: Japan's central bank has been raising rates slowly from near zero, and the yen has been weak near 158 per dollar because Japanese rates sit far below US rates.
beats.happened: The bank held at 1.25% in an 8-1 vote; board member Hajime Takata wanted a rise now. It lifted its inflation forecasts, judged underlying inflation to be in line with 2%, and sped up the sale of its stock-fund holdings.
beats.means: Saying the 2% goal is met removes a main reason to wait, so economists see a rise as soon as December and possibly more often after that. The hold itself was expected, so the yen's first gain was partly given back.
beats.fx: A clearer path to higher Japanese rates → some support for the yen, capped because the hold was expected.

impact.why: The bank says its inflation goal is met and one member already wants a rise.
A narrower gap between US and Japanese rates trims the dollar's edge over the yen.

items.watch: If spring wage talks or the December data disappoint, or the bank sounds in no hurry, the yen would lose this support.

items.headline: Oil set for fourth monthly gain as Hormuz tanker attack highlights supply risks from war
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: A tanker was hit by explosives in the Strait of Hormuz, lifting Brent crude to about $116 a barrel and putting oil on course for a fourth straight monthly gain.

beats.was: The US-Israeli war with Iran is in its eighth month, and the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been largely shut.
beats.happened: The UK's maritime security agency said a small boat attached explosives to a tanker in the strait; the attacker is unknown. Brent rose about 1% to near $116 and US crude to about $103, after Yemen's Houthi group said it struck Saudi refineries on Thursday.
beats.means: Fresh attacks on ships and Saudi sites keep the war premium in oil even as the US tries to restart talks with Iran. Brent is up about 11% this month.
beats.fx: Higher oil → support for oil exporters like the Canadian dollar, a heavier import bill for Japan and Europe.

impact.why: A new attack inside the strait adds to supply fears.
Canada exports oil, so higher prices help its currency.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so costlier crude weighs on the yen.

items.watch: A reply from Iran to the US letter seeking talks, or ships passing the strait safely, would cool prices.

items.headline: Australia's producer prices kept climbing in the September quarter
items.story_title: RBA: a fifth hike on November 3?
items.summary: Prices Australian businesses charge each other rose 1.1% in the July–September quarter and 3.6% over the year, the same yearly pace as before.

beats.was: Australia's consumer inflation came in hotter than the Reserve Bank of Australia expected this week, and markets lean heavily toward a rate rise at its November 3 meeting.
beats.happened: The producer price index, which tracks what firms pay and charge further up the supply chain, rose 1.1% in the quarter. The yearly rate held at 3.6%. Building and health-care costs rose, while manufacturing prices fell.
beats.means: Price pressure is not easing at the business level either, which keeps the case for a November rise intact. Steady, not rising, yearly growth means it adds little new.
beats.fx: Firm producer prices → support for an RBA rise and the Australian dollar, but mostly already priced.

impact.why: Sticky business prices back the case for an RBA rate rise next week.

items.watch: The RBA decision on November 3; a hold would surprise and hit the Australian dollar.

items.headline: Japan September factory output beats forecasts, but retail sales disappoint ahead of BoJ
items.story_title: Bank of Japan: when the next hike comes
items.summary: Japan's factories produced more in September than expected, but shop sales fell for a second month, giving a mixed picture hours before the Bank of Japan decides on rates.

beats.was: Japan's factory output dropped 2.4% in August, and the Bank of Japan, which holds its rate at 1.25%, wants signs the economy can cope with more rate rises.
beats.happened: Factory output rose 2.2% in September, well above the 1.3% expected, and manufacturers expect a further 5.1% gain in October. Retail sales slipped 0.7% on the month, a second fall, and were up only 2.3% on the year against 3.3% forecast.
beats.means: Industry looks to be recovering while households are spending less. That balance is unlikely to change Friday's expected hold, but weak shoppers give the bank a reason to move slowly.
beats.fx: Strong factories, soft shoppers → no clear new reason for a faster Bank of Japan → the yen waits for the decision itself.

impact.why: Better industry and weaker spending roughly cancel out before the rate decision.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan's statement on Friday and whether it mentions weak household spending as a reason for caution.

items.headline: Chicago PMI Drops to 55.3 vs 55.8 Forecast — Manufacturing Growth Slows
items.story_title: US economy: strong growth, cooling signs
items.summary: A survey of businesses around Chicago showed activity still growing in October, but more slowly than in September and a bit below forecasts.

beats.was: The US economy grew at a 3.4% yearly pace last quarter, and the Federal Reserve is weighing a rate rise in December.
beats.happened: The Chicago Business Barometer, a monthly survey of purchasing managers, fell to 55.3 from 58.8, a little under the roughly 56 economists expected. Any reading above 50 means activity is growing.
beats.means: Business in the Midwest is still expanding at a solid clip, just less briskly. It is a small sign of cooling, not a reason for the Fed to change course.
beats.fx: A slight miss on a second-tier survey barely changes the outlook for US rates, so the effect on the dollar is small.

impact.why: Slower, though still solid, business growth trims the case for more Fed rises a little.

items.watch: The national ISM manufacturing survey on Monday, November 2, which covers the whole country.

items.headline: Nasdaq faces $2 trillion wipeout in October as AI spending fears deepen
items.story_title: Wall Street: doubts over AI spending
items.summary: More than $2 trillion is set to be wiped off the Nasdaq 100 index of big US tech firms this month, as investors doubt that huge spending on artificial intelligence will pay off soon.

beats.was: US tech giants have been raising their spending plans on AI data centres for months, and those shares have carried the US stock market.
beats.happened: The Nasdaq 100 was down nearly 6% for October by Friday. Alphabet had its worst one-day fall on record after weak search-ad results, Meta plans a record $97.5 billion fund-raise, and Meta, Alphabet and Amazon all raised spending forecasts again.
beats.means: Money is leaving tech shares for safer places like US government bonds, which pushes US yields down and makes investors more cautious overall.
beats.fx: Lower US yields take some shine off the dollar, while the yen and Swiss franc tend to gain when investors get nervous.

impact.why: Money moving into US bonds pulls yields down, trimming the dollar's rate edge.
Nervous markets tend to draw money into the yen.
The franc draws shelter money when stocks fall.

items.watch: If Apple next week and Nvidia in mid-November show AI spending paying off, the selling could ease and yields recover.

items.headline: Oil flows are up as Iran war turmoil eases. Why do prices keep rising?
items.story_title: Hormuz: war risk keeps oil high
items.summary: Gulf oil exports are back above pre-war levels, yet Brent crude briefly topped $117 a barrel on Friday, because stockpiles are low, shipping costs are huge and traders fear new US strikes on Iran.

beats.was: The US war on Iran left the Strait of Hormuz, the main exit for Gulf oil, largely shut, and Brent is up more than 60% since the war began.
beats.happened: Gulf crude exports averaged about 24.6 million barrels a day in mid-October, above pre-war levels, with 40% now bypassing the strait. But world stocks are about 509 million barrels below pre-war levels, freight costs about $40 a barrel, roughly ten times normal, and October saw a record 32 attacks on ships.
beats.means: Even with oil moving again, thin stockpiles and the risk of more fighting keep prices high, and a drop back to $70 would need lasting peace and normal shipping.
beats.fx: Supports oil and the currencies of oil sellers like Canada, and weighs on big importers such as Japan and the euro area.

impact.why: Low stockpiles and costly shipping keep a floor under prices even as flows recover.
High oil prices help Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: A lasting US-Iran deal and safe shipping through Hormuz would start to bring prices down; new US strikes would lift them.

items.headline: Germany October inflation slows more than expected to 2.8%
items.story_title: Euro zone: growth holds up as prices climb
items.summary: German inflation fell to 2.8% in October from 3.3%, cooler than forecast, as energy costs rose more slowly and the underlying rate eased to 2.1%.

beats.was: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday and hinted it may raise rates in December because energy costs keep prices high. Earlier Friday, inflation in Italy and France came in hot.
beats.happened: Germany's first estimate showed prices up 2.8% from a year ago on the EU-wide measure, against 3.1% expected. Energy inflation slowed to 12.2% from 14.9%, and prices excluding food and energy rose 2.1%, down from 2.4%.
beats.means: Germany is the euro zone's biggest economy, so a cooler reading there takes some heat out of the case for a December rise, even with Italy and France running hot.
beats.fx: Softer prices in Germany → some weight on the euro, which has already been losing ground to the pound.

impact.why: Cooler German prices than expected weaken the case for a December ECB rise.

items.watch: The euro-zone-wide inflation estimate next week; a hot figure despite Germany would put the December rise back in view.

items.headline: US labor costs rise moderately in third quarter
items.story_title: Federal Reserve: the October 28 decision
items.summary: US labor costs rose 0.8% in the third quarter, exactly as forecast, and 3.4% over the year, the same pace as before.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held rates on Wednesday but left a December rise open, and Thursday's strong growth and inflation figures made one look more likely.
beats.happened: The Employment Cost Index, a broad gauge of what employers pay in wages and benefits, rose 0.8% from July to September after 0.9% in the spring. The yearly rise held at 3.4%.
beats.means: Pay is not adding new inflation pressure, so the figure neither strengthens nor weakens the case for a December rise.
beats.fx: In line with forecasts → little change for the dollar.

impact.why: Wage costs matched forecasts, so they add no new pressure either way on Fed rates.

items.watch: A sharp jump in pay growth in the next jobs report would add to the case for a December Fed rise.

items.headline: BOJ Governor Ueda's comments at news conference
items.story_title: Bank of Japan: how soon the next rate rise
items.summary: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank won't sit and wait, but stopped short of naming a date for the next rate rise, and the yen gave back some of its gains.

beats.was: Hours earlier the bank held its rate at 1.25% and said underlying inflation is now in line with its 2% goal.
beats.happened: At his press conference Ueda said the goal is not fully reached yet, that upside risks to prices have not grown sharply in the past month, and that the bank will adjust policy as needed rather than wait.
beats.means: His words keep December possible without promising it, so they added little to the morning's decision.
beats.fx: No firm signal on timing → the yen trimmed its gains, near 157.4 per dollar.

impact.why: Open to a rise but no date given, so the yen's gains faded a little.

items.watch: A clear hint of a December rise from Ueda or his deputies would give the yen a stronger lift.

items.headline: Yen steady before BOJ, AI jitters drive Treasury rally, weigh on dollar
items.story_title: Big Tech results and the AI spending boom
items.summary: Worries about how much tech companies spend on AI sent money into US government bonds, pulling yields to one-month lows and leaving the dollar a little softer as Asia opened Friday.

beats.was: Google's owner Alphabet reported results this week that revived doubts about whether huge spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and stocks fell.
beats.happened: Investors moved into safe US Treasury bonds, and the 10-year yield fell to about 4.9%, its lowest in over a month. The dollar index eased to near 101.8, the yen held near 157.8 per dollar before the Bank of Japan's decision, and the euro sat near $1.118.
beats.means: Lower US yields shrink the dollar's interest-rate edge, so a stock scare is softening the dollar rather than lifting it. The dollar is still set for a second monthly gain.
beats.fx: Falling US yields → mild pressure on the dollar; the yen waits on the Bank of Japan.

impact.why: Lower Treasury yields trim the dollar's rate edge.
Narrower US yields help the yen, but traders are waiting for the Bank of Japan.

items.watch: If US yields bounce back above 5%, or the stock selloff deepens into wider fear, the dollar's direction could change.

items.headline: Oil rises on prospects of fresh U.S. military action against Iran
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Oil rose about 0.7% in early Asian trading Friday after a report that the top US commander for the Middle East briefed President Trump on new military options against Iran.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for months, with the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut. Talks have stalled, and President Donald Trump has hinted at new strikes after the November 3 midterm elections.
beats.happened: The Wall Street Journal reported that Admiral Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command, briefed Trump on options including a return to major fighting. Brent crude rose to about $115.70 a barrel and US crude to about $102.80; both are heading for a fourth straight month of gains above 10%.
beats.means: Each sign that fighting could restart adds to the war premium in oil. Low US crude stocks and Houthi missile fire at Saudi Arabia keep supply worries alive too.
beats.fx: Talk of new US strikes → firmer oil; that helps oil exporters like Canada and weighs on big importers like Japan.

impact.why: The chance of renewed US strikes on Iran adds to supply fears.
Higher oil lifts Canada's main export earnings.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a higher bill hurts the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran accepts a deal through Qatar's mediators, or US strikes resume after the November 3 election.

items.headline: US dollar retreats despite strong GDP growth as Fed rate outlook remains uncertain
items.story_title: Fed week: the October 28 decision and December hike bets
items.summary: The dollar ended Thursday a little lower against most major currencies, even though US growth and inflation figures came in strong.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday. Two officials wanted a rise, but Fed Chair Kevin Warsh would not promise one in December.
beats.happened: Thursday's figures showed the US economy grew at a 3.4% yearly pace last quarter, above forecasts, and the Fed's preferred price gauge rose to 3.6%. Even so, the dollar index slipped about 0.2% to near 102, and the pound gained about 0.3% to near $1.336.
beats.means: Strong numbers were not enough to lift the dollar while the Fed itself stays vague about December. Traders seem to want a clear signal from the bank, not just good data, before buying more dollars.
beats.fx: Strong data but an unclear Fed → a small dollar dip; a firm hint of a December rise would likely turn it back up.

impact.why: The dollar slipped as the Fed's silence on December outweighed strong growth and price figures.
The pound was the day's best gainer against a softer dollar.

items.watch: Comments from Fed officials before the December meeting, and next week's US jobs report; a clear hint of a rise would lift the dollar.

items.headline: Euro rebounds as Lagarde signals December hike
items.story_title: ECB: the October 29 decision
items.summary: The euro won back an early loss to trade near $1.116 after European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said policymakers had talked about raising rates on Thursday before deciding to wait.

beats.was: The European Central Bank has raised its deposit rate twice this year, to 2.5%, because costly energy keeps pushing prices up. It held on Thursday, and the euro first fell to its weakest since May 2025.
beats.happened: At her press conference, Lagarde said a rise had been discussed, that inflation risks lean higher on energy costs, and that the bank has tools to calm any disorderly selling of French bonds. Markets now see a better than 80% chance of a rise on December 17. The euro, down about 0.4% earlier, ended slightly higher.
beats.means: The pause looks like a short wait, not the end of rate rises. Her stress on tighter lending and steady underlying inflation leaves some room for doubt, which is why the bounce was small.
beats.fx: A December rise looks likely again → support for the euro after its early drop; it is still near a 17-month low, so the lift is modest.

impact.why: Lagarde's word that a rise was discussed revived December hike bets and pulled the euro off its lows.

items.watch: Eurozone inflation for October, due early next week, and French bond yields; a hot price reading would firm up a December rise.

items.headline: ECB keeps rates unchanged, euro slips
items.story_title: ECB: the October 29 decision
items.summary: The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday and left a December rise possible without promising one. The euro dipped about 0.3% to near $1.11, its lowest since May 2025.

beats.was: The European Central Bank has raised its deposit rate twice this year, to 2.5%, because expensive energy is pushing prices up. The euro was already sliding on worry over France's government debt.
beats.happened: The bank held rates as expected and warned that energy costs keep the risk of higher inflation alive, so a December rise stays possible. It also noted that borrowing has become harder for firms and households, which some analysts read as a higher bar for more rises.
beats.means: The bank still leans toward tighter policy, but it did not commit, and tighter lending plus France's troubles give it reasons to wait.
beats.fx: No firm promise of a December rise → the euro slipped to a 17-month low; a clear signal later toward a rise would help it, more worry over France would push it lower.

impact.why: A hold with no promise on December, and the euro fell to its lowest since May 2025.

items.watch: European Central Bank speeches before the December 17 meeting, eurozone inflation for October, and French bond yields.

items.headline: US inflation heats up in September; consumer spending rises
items.story_title: Fed: the October 28 decision and what comes next
items.summary: The Federal Reserve's preferred price gauge rose to 3.6% a year in September, from 3.4%, mostly on gasoline. Prices outside food and energy rose 3.1%, as expected.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday and said inflation is still too high; markets were already betting on a rise in December.
beats.happened: The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.5% in September and 3.6% from a year earlier. Without food and energy it rose 0.3% on the month and 3.1% on the year, in line with forecasts. Household spending rose 0.5%, but nothing once higher prices are taken out.
beats.means: Energy is still pushing inflation up, while the underlying pace held where economists expected, so the case for a December rise stands without getting stronger.
beats.fx: Hotter headline prices → mild support for the dollar and a weight on gold; no surprise in the core figure → no big move.

impact.why: Keeps a December rate rise on the table, about 85% priced, but adds little new.
Higher odds of a US rate rise weigh on a metal that pays no interest.

items.watch: The October jobs report and October inflation figures before the Fed's December 9 decision.

items.headline: ECB President Christine Lagarde to step down next February, months before her mandate ends
items.story_title: ECB: the October 29 decision
items.summary: Christine Lagarde will leave as head of the European Central Bank on February 7, 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term ends. The search for her successor starts now.

beats.was: Lagarde has led the European Central Bank since November 2019, and talk that she might leave early had been building for months.
beats.happened: On the morning of the bank's rate decision, the bank said she will step down on February 7, 2027, giving no reason. European Council President António Costa said the choice of a successor begins at once; EU leaders pick the new head on the advice of finance ministers. Former central bank chiefs Klaas Knot of the Netherlands and Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain are often named as likely picks.
beats.means: Policy is unlikely to change because of her exit, but who replaces her, and whether they lean toward tighter or looser policy, becomes a new question for the euro in the months ahead.
beats.fx: The euro barely moved because the exit was widely expected; a successor seen as firmer on inflation → support for the euro, a softer pick → pressure.

impact.why: A leadership change at the bank that sets euro rates; the direction depends on who comes next.

items.watch: Which candidates EU finance ministers put forward, and how quickly leaders agree on a name.

items.headline: U.S. warns allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes, retaliation after midterms: AP sources
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Two diplomats told the Associated Press that the US has warned Middle East allies to brace for possible new US strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, and for Iranian attacks in return.

beats.was: The US and Iran fought earlier this year, and the Strait of Hormuz, a route for about a fifth of the world's oil, is still largely shut. The US has not struck Iran since early September, and talks helped by Qatar have stalled.
beats.happened: The diplomats said US officials told allies new strikes could last several days, and urged them to protect energy sites and other key infrastructure from Iranian retaliation. President Trump has not made a final decision. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran is still giving talks a chance.
beats.means: A second news group now backs an earlier Wall Street Journal report, so the risk of fighting after November 3 looks more real. The warning about energy sites points straight at Gulf oil supply.
beats.fx: More signs of US strikes after the election → risk to Gulf oil sites → keeps oil high, which helps Canada and weighs on Japan and Europe, and adds shelter demand for the dollar and Swiss franc.

impact.why: Allies were told to guard energy sites against Iranian retaliation.
Rising war risk draws money to the franc.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so higher fuel costs weigh on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Trump decides on strikes after November 3, or talks with Iran restart first.

items.headline: U.S. GDP Accelerates to 3.4% in Third Quarter of 2026
items.story_title: Fed: the October 28 decision and what comes next
items.summary: The US economy grew at a 3.4% yearly pace from July to September, up from 2.2% in the spring and a bit above the 3.2% forecast.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve is weighing a rate rise in December because inflation is running hot; a strong economy makes that easier to do.
beats.happened: The first official estimate of third-quarter growth showed business investment, especially in computers and equipment, household spending and government spending all rising. Falling exports and rising imports held growth back a little.
beats.means: The economy is strong enough that a December rate rise would not obviously hurt it, which keeps the Fed's tighter path in place.
beats.fx: A growth beat → mild support for the dollar; the dollar barely moved because a December rise was already expected.

impact.why: Strong growth backs the case for a December Fed rise that markets already expect.

items.watch: The second estimate of third-quarter growth on November 25 and the October jobs report.

items.headline: Aussie Gains as Hot Inflation Fuels RBA Tightening Bets
items.story_title: RBA: a fifth hike on November 3?
items.summary: The Australian dollar held above 70.5 US cents on Thursday after hot inflation figures. Markets now give about an 85% chance that the Reserve Bank of Australia raises its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, November 3.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised its rate four times this year, to 4.6%. On Wednesday, official figures showed prices up 4.3% from a year earlier in September, above the 4.2% expected.
beats.happened: The Australian dollar firmed to about 70.55 US cents. Bets on a quarter-point rise next Tuesday jumped from about 60% before the figures to about 85%, and bets on another rise early next year grew too. Underlying inflation for the July-September quarter, 3.7%, is well above the bank's own forecast.
beats.means: Australia now looks set to keep raising rates while some neighbours pause. That rate edge is what is holding the currency up.
beats.fx: Another rate rise all but priced → support for the Australian dollar; a weak US inflation reading later on Thursday would add to it, a hot one would test it.

impact.why: Higher odds of a rate rise next week, but most of it is already priced.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of Australia's decision on Tuesday, November 3, and whether Governor Michele Bullock hints at more after it.

items.headline: Oil falls as diplomacy hopes outweigh Middle East escalation fears
items.story_title: US-Iran war: talks vs new strikes
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 1% to near $114 a barrel on Thursday morning in London as fresh peace efforts between the US and Iran took some heat out of prices. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz kept the drop small.

beats.was: Oil has been above $100 for weeks because the war between the US, Israel and Iran has largely shut the Strait of Hormuz, the sea lane for about a fifth of the world's oil. Yemen's Houthi rebels, who back Iran, said on Tuesday they hit Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery.
beats.happened: Brent slipped $1.27 to about $114 and US crude fell 1.5% to about $101 by mid-morning in London. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance wrote to a senior Iranian security official to restart talks, and Qatar has put a new draft deal to Iran. But a Saudi-led coalition said it shot down a missile fired at eastern Saudi Arabia early Thursday, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit sea mines south of Hormuz.
beats.means: Talk of a deal is enough to shave a little off the war premium, but every new attack shows supply is still at risk. Worry that the US could strike Iran after its November 3 midterm elections keeps buyers from leaving.
beats.fx: Talks gain ground → oil eases → small relief for oil importers like the euro and yen, less help for the Canadian dollar; new attacks or US strikes → oil jumps back.

impact.why: Peace efforts trim the war premium, though attacks limit the fall.
Slightly lower oil means a little less support for a big Canadian export.
Japan imports nearly all its fuel, so cheaper oil eases pressure on the yen.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers Qatar's draft or the Vance letter, and any new Houthi strike on Saudi oil sites or tanker attacks near Hormuz.

items.headline: Tokyo core inflation exceeds BOJ target in October
items.story_title: Bank of Japan: when the next hike comes
items.summary: Prices in Tokyo, an early guide to all of Japan, rose 2.6% in October from a year before, still above the Bank of Japan's 2% goal. A deeper measure that leaves out food and fuel cooled to 2.6% from 2.9%.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan raised its rate in September to 1.25%, its highest in 31 years, and decides again later on Friday, October 30. It is expected to hold, but has said it will keep raising rates if inflation runs too hot. The yen is weak near 158 per dollar.
beats.happened: Tokyo prices excluding fresh food rose 2.6% in October, as forecast, after 2.7% in September. The measure that also leaves out fuel, which the bank watches for the underlying trend, slowed to 2.6% from 2.9%.
beats.means: Inflation is still above target, so the case for another rise stays alive, but the cooling in the underlying trend gives the bank less reason to sound urgent on Friday.
beats.fx: Inflation above 2% but easing → no push for a faster Bank of Japan → little help for the yen before the decision.

impact.why: Still above target, but the underlying trend cooled, so it neither adds nor removes much from December hike bets.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan's decision and new forecasts on Friday, then Governor Kazuo Ueda's press conference for a hint about December.

items.headline: Middle East War: Saudi intercepts Houthi missile as four tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
items.story_title: Iran war: the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Iran says four tankers caught fire after hitting its mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi Arabia shot down Houthi missiles fired at its capital, Riyadh.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, has been largely shut since Iran's war with the US began this year, and Iran has mined it. Yemen's Houthi rebels, allied with Iran, have been firing at Saudi Arabia.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers using a southern route through the strait hit mines and caught fire within a day; Iran's army later reported a fourth stuck and burning east of the strait. Iran says the ships had switched off their tracking and ignored its warnings; no one else has confirmed the details. Saudi air defences also brought down two Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh, and Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, warned that any Israeli-led attack in the Gulf would badly hurt world markets.
beats.means: Ships trying to slip through the strait are being hit, so even the small flow of oil still getting out is at risk. Together with missiles at Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, this keeps the war premium in oil despite talk of peace efforts.
beats.fx: Tankers hit and Saudi Arabia targeted → more risk to Gulf oil supply → support for oil prices, which helps Canada and weighs on Japan and Europe, and adds shelter demand for the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Four tankers reported burning and missiles at Riyadh hit the little Gulf supply still moving.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so higher prices hurt its trade balance.
War news draws shelter money into the franc.

items.watch: Whether shipping firms or Western navies confirm the tanker strikes, and any further Houthi attacks on Saudi oil sites.

items.headline: US-Iran Deal Nears as Envoy Credits Qatar, Pakistan for Mediation Efforts
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Tom Barrack, a senior US envoy, said Washington and Tehran are very close to a first understanding on how to calm the war, and called for a pause in fighting. Iran called the latest ideas sent through Qatar unacceptable.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war for about eight months, and the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil route, is still largely shut. Reports this week said the US has warned Gulf allies to prepare for new strikes on Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections.
beats.happened: Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria, told CNN on Thursday the two sides were very close to an initial deal on a process to bring tensions down, and thanked Qatar and Pakistan for their help. He asked for a time-out in the fighting. A senior Iranian official, though, rejected the latest proposals passed on by Qatar.
beats.means: Washington is sending peace signals and strike warnings in the same week, so neither outcome is settled. Iran's rejection means the hopeful words are not yet a deal.
beats.fx: Talk of a deal → a little less war premium in oil and less shelter demand; Iran's rejection keeps that effect small.

impact.why: Hopeful US words trim the war premium, but Iran's rejection limits the effect.
Less talk of war means a little less need for shelter.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers with its own proposal, and any US decision on strikes after the November 3 elections.

items.headline: Fed holds rates in a split vote; Warsh keeps December open and changes the meeting calendar
items.story_title: Federal Reserve: the October 28 decision
items.summary: The US Federal Reserve kept its rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, as expected, with two officials voting for a hike. At his press briefing, Chair Kevin Warsh made no promise on December and said that from 2027 one meeting a year will skip the rate vote.

beats.was: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, because the Iran war pushed fuel prices up and US inflation reached 3.7% in September. Markets saw a pause this time as near certain and were already pricing a likely hike at the December 8-9 meeting.
beats.happened: The vote was 10-2: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point hike. The statement called growth strong and said more information will help the Fed set the right level of rates. At the briefing, Chair Kevin Warsh repeated that line and announced that from 2027 one of the eight yearly meetings will be a strategy session with no rate vote and no statement, rising to two in 2028.
beats.means: December is not settled: the Fed wants to see more data first, but two votes for a hike show pressure inside the bank. Markets still see about an 86% chance of a December hike, up from 78% on Tuesday. Fewer voting meetings from 2027 mean fewer dates on which rates can change.
beats.fx: Pause with hawkish votes, no promise on December → hike odds stay high but depend on the data → the dollar keeps its rate support and stays near its high for the year, waiting on Thursday's figures.

impact.why: Expected pause; hike votes and high December odds support it, while Warsh's wait-for-data tone holds it back.
No hike today helps gold a little; a likely December hike still weighs on it.

items.watch: Thursday's US figures: third-quarter growth and the September PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge; a hot reading firms up December.
